metadata.note: The Vermont Central Railroad, chartered Oct 31 1843 to cross the state from Windsor on the Connecticut River to Burlington on Lake Champlain. Construction began Dec 15 1845. Interestingly, the original plan ran the main line through Montpelier itself, but the difficulty of building through the Williamstown Gulf south of Barre, plus land interests of promoter Charles Paine in Northfield, pushed the chosen route west through Northfield instead -- leaving the state capital to be served by a short branch off the main line (Montpelier Junction). The line opened in stages: White River Junction-Bethel June 26 1848; Roxbury Sept 17 1848; Northfield Oct 10 1848; the southern Windsor-Hartford/White River Jct segment along the Connecticut River Feb 13 1849; the Montpelier branch (from Montpelier Junction) June 20 1849 -- the date Vermont's capital got passenger rail; Middlesex Aug 30 1849; Waterbury Sept 29 1849; and the full line through to Burlington Dec 31 1849. The company struggled financially (an ill-advised lease of the Rutland Railroad, then the Panic of 1873) and was renamed the Central Vermont Railroad on Nov 2 1872 ahead of an 1873 bankruptcy reorganization -- see montrealer.geojson and amtrak.geojson's 'Vermonter' for this corridor's later Central Vermont/Canadian National/Amtrak history, not re-modeled here. Geometry was re-traced from OpenStreetMap on 2026-08-27, replacing the straight-line town-to-town waypoints this layer previously carried (8 points for the main line, 2 for the branch); it is now 309 points of real track centreline over the New England Central, the successor operator on the same alignment. See each feature's geometry_quality. The same pass split the 1848 portion into its own feature: the old main-line feature drew the entire Windsor-Burlington line from 1848, when in fact only White River Junction-Northfield had opened that year.

metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
metadata.geometry_audit_20260827: Re-traced from OpenStreetMap. Main line 8 points -> 309 points, 115.0 mi; Montpelier branch 2 points -> 13 points, 1.55 mi, and now drawn from the real junction rather than a guessed one. A third feature was added for the 1848-only White River Junction-Northfield section so no year asserts unbuilt track. Zero backtracking in either trace. Neither feature previously carried a geometry_quality field at all, which Rule 2 requires.
metadata.successor_added_20260827: Three Central Vermont features were added on 2026-08-27 to close a gap this layer created: the Vermont Central features stop at the November 2 1872 rename, and nothing carried the corridor forward, so BURLINGTON went blank on the map from 1873 until the Rutland Railroad feature picks it up in 1892, and the main line through Montpelier Junction went blank from 1873 until the Montrealer in 1924. The successor is drawn on identical geometry per CLAUDE.md Rule 4, split into three features because the three legs lost passenger service in three different years: the Burlington branch in 1938, the Montpelier branch somewhere in 1925-1938, and the main line in 1966. Drawing one uniform 1873-1966 feature over all of it would have asserted Burlington service that ended 28 years earlier.
metadata.company_naming_note: The 1873-1898 features carry company 'Central Vermont Railway' although the company was legally the Central Vermont RAILROAD until the 1898 reorganisation. This is deliberate: CLAUDE.md Rule 4 says different name strings for the same real company count as one company and should be normalised before comparing, and Railroad -> Railway across a bankruptcy reorganisation is that case. Using one string keeps the whole 1873-1966 succession on the single #8C5E3C already used for Central Vermont Railway in new_london_northern_railroad.geojson, from which this colour was pulled programmatically. The segment notes name the Railroad era explicitly.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, replacing the straight-line town-to-town waypoints this layer previously carried. Shortest-path routing over OSM relation 9048140, the New England Central Railroad -- the direct operating successor on this exact alignment -- whose ways are tagged old_railway_operator=CN (Canadian National, which owned the Central Vermont). The Essex Junction-Burlington and Montpelier Junction-Montpelier ends are not in that relation and came from Overpass bbox extracts; gaps between disconnected fragments were bridged only where the fragments were already in separate components, the largest such bridge being 350 m in the multi-track Burlington terminal area. No straight-line approximation remains. CAVEAT (CLAUDE.md Rule 2): this is the MODERN New England Central alignment drawn back to 1848. The corridor and town sequence are the Vermont Central's own and the line has seen little relocation, but 19th-century realignments have not been backed out and no period valuation map was consulted, so the earliest years are drawn on later track wherever the alignment moved. Traced 52.9 mi, cut from the main-line trace at White River Junction and at Northfield.

segments.note: The first part of the Vermont Central to carry passengers, and for about a year the only part: White River Junction to Bethel opened June 26 1848, Roxbury September 17 1848 and Northfield October 10 1848. Nothing south of White River Junction or north of Northfield was open yet -- the Windsor end did not follow until February 13 1849 and Burlington not until December 31 1849. Drawn as its own feature so that the 1848 map does not assert track that had not been built; the full-line feature now starts in 1849. Frequency estimated.

segments.note: The Vermont Central was renamed the Central Vermont Railroad on November 2 1872 and went through an 1873 bankruptcy; the trains kept running over the same rails. This is the through route -- Windsor, White River Junction, Randolph, Northfield, Montpelier Junction, Waterbury and Essex Junction -- and it is what put Montpelier back on this map for the years after the Vermont Central ends. CV trains ran south of Windsor over the Boston & Maine to Brattleboro and on toward New London. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the November 2 1872 rename and the 1873 bankruptcy are sourced below; the 1893 Pathfinder timetable in the branchline.uk list confirms passenger stops at Windsor, Hartland, White River Junction, Randolph, Northfield, Montpelier Junction, Waterbury and Essex Junction in this era. The headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: Reorganised as the Central Vermont Railway in 1898 after the 1896 bankruptcy, with the Grand Trunk taking majority control and Canadian National succeeding it; the CV stayed a CN subsidiary until the 1995 spin-off that created today's New England Central. Passenger service over this main line ran to the end: the branchline.uk list shows stops at Randolph, Northfield, Waterbury and Essex Junction in the 1916, 1924, 1939 and 1953 timetables. The CV's own overnight Vermonter (St. Albans - White River Junction) ran 1940 to November 5 1965, and Vermont's last regular Central Vermont passenger service ended September 3 1966. Frequency estimated. The Montrealer and later Amtrak's Vermonter cover this corridor's post-1924 through service in montrealer.geojson and amtrak.geojson; this feature is the CV's own trains.
sources: Segment-level: the 1896 bankruptcy, 1898 reorganisation, Grand Trunk/CN control, the CV Vermonter's 1940-1965 span and the September 3 1966 end of regular service are sourced below; per-station timetable appearances are from the branchline.uk Vermont list. The headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: Burlington kept its Central Vermont trains after the 1872 rename, over the 7.7 miles from Essex Junction through Winooski. This is the stretch that was missing from the map: the Vermont Central features stop in 1872 and the Rutland Railroad feature does not begin until 1892, leaving Burlington blank for two decades it was in fact served. Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the branchline.uk list shows Winooski, on this branch, in the 1850, 1876, 1893, 1916 and 1924 timetables. The headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: Central Vermont passenger service to Burlington ended on June 17 1938 with the discontinuance of the Burlington - Cambridge Junction mixed train. The branch is drawn to 1938 and no further: after that Burlington's passenger service was the Rutland Railroad's alone, until the Rutland strike of June 26 1953 ended passenger service to the city entirely for 69 years. Freight continued on this branch long after 1938 -- context, not drawn service (Rule 1). Frequency estimated.
sources: Segment-level: the June 17 1938 end of CV passenger service to Burlington is from the Burlington Union Station history; the branchline.uk list independently shows Winooski present in the 1924 timetable and absent from the 1939 Official Guide, which agrees. The headway is NOT sourced.

segments.note: The Central Vermont kept running trains down the short branch from Montpelier Junction into Montpelier itself, where the line continued to Barre and Williamstown (the Barre end is drawn separately in montpelier_wells_river_railroad.geojson). DATE CAUTION: the drawn end year is a floor, not a sourced date -- the branchline.uk list shows the downtown Montpelier station in the 1893, 1916 and 1924 timetables and absent from the 1939 Official Guide, so service certainly existed in 1924 and had gone by 1939. It is drawn to 1925 so as not to assert years that are not evidenced; the real end is somewhere in 1925-1938. Through passengers used Montpelier Junction on the main line, which kept its stop into the Amtrak era. Frequency estimated.
